question: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2025/327 on the European Health Data Space provides for the extensive use of medical data, including for research, statistics and the development of new technologies. At the same time, its implementation will require significant investment in national IT systems, cybersecurity and administration. With that in mind: 1.

How will the Commission ensure that patients’ right to object to the secondary use of their data is simple, effective and easily accessible, and that exceptions to this right do not lead to restrictions being effectively imposed on it?

Does the Commission have a detailed estimate of the costs of implementing the European Health Data Space (EHDS) for Poland, including the costs incurred by hospitals, clinics and public administration, and what proportion of these expenses can be covered by EU funds?

Why is a comprehensive evaluation of the functioning of the Regulation not foreseen until 2035, and does the Commission intend to carry out an earlier evaluation covering costs, the effectiveness of data protection, security incidents and the impact of the new obligations on national healthcare systems?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) Under Article 71 of Regulation (EU) 2025/327 on the European Health Data Space, (EHDS)1, Member States must provide ‘accessible and easily understandable’ mechanisms for natural persons to exercise their right to opt out from having their personal electronic health data being made available for secondary use. Member States may provide for exceptions to the right to opt out under limited circumstances restricted to cases where data access is requested by public bodies for critical public interest (e.g., health threats) and rigorous justification is required. These exceptions must in particular be necessary and proportionate, maintaining all safeguards of Chapter IV of the EHDS Regulation like re-identification prohibitions. The Commission has provided EU-wide cost estimates in the EHDS impact assessment accompanying its proposal2. While no estimate specific to Poland is available, implementation costs are expected to broadly scale with population, with some economies of scale (i.e. degressive costs). EU funding may support implementation through relevant Union programmes, such as the EU4Health programme, subject to their conditions. Pursuant to Better Regulation guidelines3, ex-post evaluation requires data on the application of the legislation over a period of at least three to four years, as results and impacts take time to materialise. Given the application timelines of the EHDS, an overall review is scheduled for 2035, and a targeted review, including on the opt out for secondary use mechanism, for 2033, in accordance with Article 102 of the EHDS Regulation.
